acts.title: How would you describe them?
text: A few years ago an advertising campaign asked a group of women to do something unusual. Each one sat behind a curtain and described her own face, honestly, to a forensic artist she could not see. He drew what she said. Then a stranger who had met her that morning described the same face, and he drew that too.

The two sketches were placed side by side. In almost every case the description from the stranger was more positive — often far more positive. One woman had described her own face as closed off, and fatter and sadder than it really was. The stranger described the same woman as having a thin face and bright eyes.

The campaign was selling beauty products, and it is fair to be sceptical about that. But the finding itself has been repeated in less commercial studies. We are consistently worse at describing ourselves than a stranger is, and the gap is much bigger for women than for men.

Part of the reason is that we do not look at our own faces the way we look at other people’s. A stranger sees a whole face for three seconds. We see one detail at a time, in a mirror, every day, for years: the double chin that is not nearly as obvious as we think, the grey hair, the eyebrow that is slightly higher than the other one.

The most useful thing in the whole experiment is not the drawings. It is what happened when the women were shown the two sketches together. Almost nobody argued that the stranger was wrong. They simply said, quietly, that they had not expected the difference to be that big.

items.s: Each woman described her own face without being able to see the artist.
The strangers had known the women for years.
The strangers’ descriptions were generally more positive.
The writer accepts the campaign uncritically.
According to the text, the gap is bigger for women than for men.
Most of the women argued that the stranger’s sketch was wrong.

write.q: Describe two people you know well without naming them, and compare them. Use at least one much/far + comparative, one not nearly as … as, one by far the + superlative, and one slightly.
write.model: The first has short, curly hair that is going grey at the sides, thick eyebrows and a bit of stubble he never quite removes. The second is clean-shaven, with straight shoulder-length hair he dyes far darker than his natural colour. Physically they are not nearly as different as they think: both are well-built, both slightly overweight, both about the same height. The real gap is in how they use it. The first is by far the more relaxed of the two — he wears the same three shirts and has never once mentioned his appearance to me. The second spends slightly longer in front of a mirror than he would ever admit.

speak.q: Describe somebody in the room, or somebody you both know, without saying who it is. Use two comparisons. Let your partner guess.
speak.model: She’s got shoulder-length hair, a bit of a fringe, and she’s slightly taller than most people here. She’s by far the quietest person on the team, and she’s not nearly as serious as she looks — she laughs at everything, just very quietly.
